n: The prophecy against Babylon continues. God will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon and against “Leb-kamai”—a coded name for Chaldea.

f.w: them that rise up against me
f.g: Hebrew Leb-qamai, “heart of my adversaries”—an atbash cipher for Kasdim, Chaldea (compare “Sheshach,” verse 41).

n: God will send “winnowers” to scatter Babylon like chaff and empty her land, attacking from every side in her day of trouble.

f.g: Winnowers—workers who toss grain in the wind to blow away the chaff.

n: Don’t let her archers draw their bows or her soldiers put on armor; spare none of her young men—destroy her whole army.
The slain will fall throughout Babylonia, pierced through in her streets.
Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, even though their land was full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel. God’s covenant outlasts their failures.
Flee from Babylon! Save your lives; don’t be destroyed in her punishment. This is the time of the Lord’s vengeance. Modern revelation echoes this call to flee spiritual Babylon.

f.w: Flee out of the midst of Babylon

n: Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, making the whole earth drunk; the nations drank her wine and went mad. God used her to deliver his judgment, but she is accountable for her cruelty.
Suddenly Babylon has fallen and shattered! Wail for her; bring balm for her wounds—maybe she can be healed.
“We tried to heal Babylon, but she can’t be healed. Let’s leave her and go home—her guilt reaches the heavens.”
The exiles respond: the Lord has vindicated us; let’s go tell in Zion what our God has done.

f.g: Our vindication—God has shown we were in the right.

n: Sharpen the arrows! Fill the quivers! God has stirred up the kings of the Medes to destroy Babylon—his vengeance for his temple.

f.g: The Medes, later united with Persia under Cyrus, helped conquer Babylon.

n: Raise the signal against Babylon’s walls, strengthen the guard, post watchmen, set ambushes—the Lord has planned it and will do it.
You who live by many waters, rich in treasure—your end has come, the thread of your life is cut. Babylon lay on the Euphrates, surrounded by canals.

f.w: O thou that dwellest upon many waters

f.g: Possibly “the thread of your life is cut off,” like a weaver cutting finished cloth.

n: The Lord swears by himself: he will fill Babylon with enemies as many as locusts, and they will shout in triumph over her.
Verses 15–19 repeat a hymn from chapter 10: the true God made the earth by his power, founded the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding—unlike Babylon’s idols.

f.w: He hath made the earth by his power

n: When he speaks, the heavens roar with water; he lifts clouds from the ends of the earth, makes lightning for the rain, and brings wind from his storehouses.
Every idol-maker is shown to be foolish; their metal images are frauds with no breath of life.

f.w: there is no breath in them

n: Idols are worthless, objects of mockery; when judgment comes, they will perish.
But the “Portion of Jacob”—Israel’s God—is nothing like them. He made everything, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name.

f.g: A title for God, who is Israel’s inheritance and treasure.

n: God addresses his “war club,” the instrument he uses to smash nations and kingdoms. In context this was Babylon herself; now her own ruin is near (some read it as Cyrus or Israel).
With it God shatters horses, riders, chariots, and charioteers…
…men and women, old and young, young men and young women…
…shepherds and flocks, farmers and oxen, governors and officials. The ninefold “break in pieces” hammers home the totality of the destruction.
God will repay Babylon and its people, before your eyes, for all the evil they did in Zion.

f.w: all their evil that they have done in Zion

n: “I am against you, destroying mountain,” says God. He will roll Babylon down from its heights like a burned-out volcano. Babylon was flat, so “mountain” pictures its towering power and perhaps its great temple-tower.
No one will take even a cornerstone or foundation stone from her ruins; she will be desolate forever.

Raise a banner, blow the trumpet, summon nations against her: Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz—peoples of the northern mountains (around modern Armenia) under Median control. Appoint a commander; bring horses like swarming locusts.

f.g: Urartu, the region around Lake Van in eastern Turkey and Armenia.
The Manneans, south of Lake Urmia in northwest Iran.

n: Prepare the nations—the kings of the Medes, their governors, officials, and all their subject lands.
The land trembles and writhes, for the Lord’s purpose against Babylon stands: to make it a desolate land.
Babylon’s warriors have stopped fighting and huddle in their fortresses; their strength is gone. Her homes are burning and the bars of her gates are broken.
Runner after runner, messenger after messenger, races to tell the king that his city has been taken from end to end.

f.w: his city is taken at one end

n: The river crossings are seized, the reed marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.

f.g: Reed marshes, perhaps used as defenses.

n: Babylon is like a threshing floor being stamped down before harvest; soon her “harvest” of judgment will come.

f.g: A hard-packed area where harvested grain was trampled to separate it from the stalks.

n: Jerusalem speaks: “Nebuchadnezzar devoured me, crushed me, emptied me like a jar, swallowed me like a sea monster, stuffed himself with my delicacies, and spit me out.”
“May the violence done to me be on Babylon,” Zion says; “May my blood be on the Chaldeans,” Jerusalem says—a cry for justice.

f.w: my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea

n: God answers: I will plead your case and avenge you. I will dry up Babylon’s “sea” and springs—the Euphrates and its canals that were her lifeblood.

f.w: I will dry up her sea

n: Babylon will become rubble heaps, a haunt of jackals, a horror and a byword, empty of people.
Babylon’s nobles roar together like lions and growl like lion cubs—ravenous and proud at their feasts.

While they are heated with appetite, God will set a feast for them and make them drunk, so they fall into a sleep they never wake from. Daniel 5 describes Belshazzar’s feast on the night Babylon fell.
God will lead them down like lambs, rams, and goats to the slaughter.
How Sheshach (Babylon) has been captured! The pride of the whole earth seized! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!
The sea has risen over Babylon; she is covered by its roaring waves—the flood of invading armies.

f.w: The sea is come up upon Babylon

n: Her towns become a dry, desolate wasteland where no one lives or even travels.
God will punish Bel (Marduk) in Babylon and make him vomit up what he swallowed—the nations, people, and temple treasures. Nations will no longer stream to him, and Babylon’s wall will fall.

f.w: that which he hath swallowed up

n: “My people, get out of her! Save yourselves from the Lord’s fierce anger.” The call to leave Babylon is a theme carried into the New Testament and modern revelation.

f.w: My people, go ye out of the midst of her

n: Don’t lose heart or panic at the rumors that will come year after year—violence in the land, ruler against ruler. Upheaval will precede the end.

f.w: a rumour shall both come one year

n: The days are coming when God will judge Babylon’s idols; the whole land will be shamed, and its slain will fall within it.
Heaven and earth and all in them will sing for joy over Babylon’s fall, when destroyers come from the north.
Babylon must fall for Israel’s slain, just as the slain of all the earth fell because of Babylon.
You who escaped the sword, go—don’t linger! Remember the Lord from far away, and keep Jerusalem in your heart.

f.w: let Jerusalem come into your mind

n: The exiles reply: “We are ashamed and disgraced, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the Lord’s house.”

f.w: strangers are come into the sanctuaries

n: God answers: the days are coming when I will judge her idols, and her wounded will groan throughout the land.

Even if Babylon climbed to heaven and fortified her lofty heights, destroyers would still come from God. Babylon’s towering temple-tower recalls the original tower of Babel, built to “reach unto heaven.”

f.w: Though Babylon should mount up to heaven

n: Listen! A cry from Babylon—the sound of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans.
The Lord is destroying Babylon and silencing her noisy din, though the enemy’s waves roar like great waters.

f.g: Babylon’s loud bustle, the noise of a great city.

n: The destroyer has come; her warriors are captured and their bows broken, for the Lord is a God of recompense who will surely repay.
God will make Babylon’s officials, wise men, governors, officers, and warriors drunk, and they will sleep forever—declares the King, the Lord of hosts.
Babylon’s massive walls will be leveled and her high gates burned. The nations’ labor to build her ends only in fire—they wear themselves out for nothing.

f.g: Ancient writers described Babylon’s walls as wide enough for chariots to drive on top.

f.w: the people shall labour in vain

n: A narrative postscript: Jeremiah gave instructions to Seraiah, Baruch’s brother, who traveled with (or for) King Zedekiah to Babylon in his fourth year (about 594/593 BC). Seraiah was the quartermaster in charge of the king’s lodging.

f.g: Hebrew sar menuchah—“quartermaster,” the officer in charge of rest-stops.

n: Jeremiah wrote on a scroll all the disaster that would come on Babylon—the words recorded here.
He told Seraiah: when you reach Babylon, look around and read all these words aloud.
Then pray: “Lord, you have declared that you will cut off this place so that nothing lives here, and it will be desolate forever.”
When you finish reading, tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates.
And say, “So Babylon will sink and never rise again because of the disaster God brings.” The book adds: “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah”—chapter 52 is a historical appendix.

f.w: Thus far are the words of Jeremiah
f.g: An editorial note marking the end of Jeremiah’s own prophecies.
